name: Thalita Regina Terpilauskas de Sa
title: AI Isn’t Magic—But It Can Deliver Remarkable Results
abstract:
Artificial intelligence is often presented as a magical solution capable of solving any business problem. However, many organizations begin their AI initiatives without a clearly defined use case, reliable data, or a realistic understanding of what the technology can deliver. This talk explores two of the most common challenges in enterprise AI adoption: the gap between business expectations and technical reality, and the lack of structured, consistent, and contextualized data. It also discusses the role of technical professionals in transforming broad AI ambitions into measurable and achievable solutions.
Finally, I will present a real-world predictive analytics project developed for the Brazilian consortium market. The case demonstrates how understanding the business problem, preparing the data, and selecting the right technical approach increased prediction accuracy from approximately 55% to 91.5%, turning an abstract AI initiative into a practical decision-support solution.
bio: Thalita Regina Terpilauskas de Sa is a Business Intelligence, Data Analytics, and Automation professional with over 12 years of experience developing data-driven solutions for international organizations. Throughout her career, she has worked at leading global companies, including Louis Dreyfus Company, COFCO International, and Cargill. She is the founder and CEO of Riverstone Insights, a US-based data and AI consulting company that provides Business Intelligence, data analytics, automation, and AI solutions to clients such as HP, Italkraft, and DirectCon. Her expertise includes Power BI, SQL, Python, machine learning, predictive analytics, and business process automation. She recently completed the MIT IDSS Data Science and Machine Learning Program and focuses on transforming complex business challenges into practical, measurable technology solutions.

name: Marcelo B San Martin
title: The Great AI Role Rewrite
abstract:
AI is no longer only automating tasks; it is beginning to rewrite the roles people play at work and in everyday life. As LLMs become collaborators, advisers, tutors, creators, and interfaces to knowledge, the value of many human roles is shifting from producing every output ourselves to directing AI systems, exercising judgment, validating results, and deciding what should not be delegated.
This talk explores the changes already visible in software teams, management, education, creative work, and daily decision-making—and what they suggest about the broader societal transformation ahead. It also examines the risks that come with convenience, including weakened critical thinking, blurred accountability, and growing dependence on systems we do not fully understand.
Rather than treating AI as simply another productivity tool, the talk presents it as the beginning of a wider redesign of work, institutions, and human identity. Attendees will leave with a practical framework for deciding what to delegate to AI, what should remain under human control, and which capabilities we need to strengthen as our roles continue to evolve.
bio: Marcelo B. San Martin is a software engineer and QA automation leader with more than 13 years of experience, including work with Salesforce, PayPal, and Blizzard Entertainment. In recent years, he has focused on applied AI, LLM-powered systems, agentic workflows, and using AI to transform software engineering and quality practices. He also creates educational content exploring the AI revolution and its impact on work, creativity, critical thinking, and everyday life.

name: Leon Achata
title: RAG Is Not a Search Problem
abstract:
Modern RAG systems are often reduced to a simple pipeline: embed documents, perform vector search, retrieve the top-k chunks, and send them to an LLM. In practice, retrieval is rarely that simple. Exact identifiers, technical terminology, semantic paraphrases, lost document context, and multi-step questions can all expose weaknesses in a purely vector-based approach.
This talk explores how modern retrieval systems move beyond basic semantic search through hybrid retrieval, combining sparse and dense methods, contextual retrieval, reranking, query decomposition, and adaptive or agentic retrieval. Rather than presenting a single “best” architecture, we will examine the trade-offs between relevance, recall, latency, cost, and complexity, and look at when each technique is actually useful.
The central idea is simple: a RAG system does not need to find the most similar chunks; it needs to retrieve the right evidence for the question. We will build this idea step by step and show how retrieval quality, rather than simply choosing a more powerful LLM, can determine the quality of the final answer.
bio: Leon Achata is a Generative AI Engineer focused on building production-grade LLM applications, RAG systems, and intelligent agents. He currently works on enterprise GenAI solutions at Apple via TCS, designing LLM-powered workflows, retrieval systems, and agent orchestration for large-scale international environments. Previously, he worked on multi-agent systems, RAG pipelines, and AI infrastructure across AWS and other cloud platforms. His background combines software engineering, AI/ML, and biomedical engineering, giving him a practical perspective on applying LLMs to complex real-world problems.

name: Josefina R. Casanova
title: From PDFs to Production RAG: Lessons from Building Document Pipelines with Docling
abstract:
Large Language Models have become remarkably capable, yet many AI projects still struggle to deliver reliable results. The problem is often not the model itself, but the quality of the information being provided to it.
In this session, we'll take a practical look at document intelligence for production AI systems. Through real-world examples and a live demo using open source tools, we'll compare different approaches for transforming complex documents into structured knowledge ready for retrieval-augmented generation (RAG).
Attendees will leave with practical techniques for improving retrieval quality, reducing hallucinations, and building more trustworthy AI systems. The session is tool-agnostic and highly practical, focused on lessons that can be immediately applied to real projects.
bio: Josefina Casanova is a Data & AI Architect at IBM and a Computer Science Engineer passionate about using technology to solve real problems. She spends her days working at the intersection of AI, data and business, helping organizations build solutions that turn messy data into systems that work in production. A lifelong learner, she regularly speaks at tech events, hosts podcasts, and enjoys sharing lessons learned from building with emerging technologies.

name: Joaquin Bonifacino
title: Long Running Agents: The Harness Is the Product
abstract:
Most agent demos run for thirty seconds. Production agents run for hours, and almost everything that breaks at that timescale has nothing to do with the model. Drawn from building an agentic data-QA engine running at 20B+ tokens per week in production.
Why long-running agents fail: context degradation, silent tool failure, unrecoverable state, cost drift, and why demos never catch them.
How harness design answers each one: compaction and memory, per-role model routing, sandboxed execution, checkpointing and recovery.
Where to start: what to build first moving an agent from demo to production, and what to instrument on day one.
bio: AI/ML Engineer at Zyte, technical lead for LLMNL, an AI-powered data-QA engine running agentic workloads at 20B+ tokens per week. Previously led Promtior's Augmented Behaviors Lab (applied R&D in agent memory, voice and multimodal). Teaches Applied AI at ORT University, Montevideo.

name: Ben Sterne
title: Beyond Vibe Coding: How AI is Changing Development Cycles
abstract: Just a few years ago, all new software was designed and coded by humans. Today, AI tools like Claude Code, Codex, and GitHub Copilot are reshaping how software is built from the ground up. This talk explores how adopting an AI-native product development cycle transformed our team's workflow and boosted productivity. We will examine the specific engineering patterns, automated verification loops, and team workflows required to move reliably beyond informal 'vibe coding' into production-grade AI development.
bio: Ben Sterne is the Product Lead for AI initiatives at Match My Email, exploring applied AI in the CRM space. He is an early adopter of AI technologies and built the first AI prototypes with top product and design executives at Salesforce and Slack to guide their AI strategies. He comes from a product design and data science background, building upon successful products as well as building new features and products from scratch. Day-to-day, he is building AI tools, drawing on 10 years of experience in the tech space working with companies like Slack, Salesforce, Sonos, and Google.

name: Axel Labruna & Maika de Jesus Esteves
photo: Axel Labruna & Maika de Jesus Esteves.png
title: AgentOps: The future is here
abstract: What if the next leap in efficiency in DevSecOps didn’t come from more tools, but from agents capable of reasoning, coordinating, and executing on our behalf? Agent-based artificial intelligence is no longer just a futuristic promise: it’s already changing the way we design, automate, and scale engineering workflows. In this talk, we’ll explore how AgentOps enables us to take AI agents from an interesting demo to real, governable, and impact-driven architectures. We’ll present agent-based architectures applied to DevSecOps scenarios, demonstrating how to design agents with clear responsibilities, explicit contracts, traceability, and collaboration mechanisms. We’ll also review design patterns for building more robust, reusable, and secure solutions. Through practical examples and demos based on real-world developments, we’ll see how these approaches can accelerate activities such as analysis, artifact generation, validation, code review, documentation, security, and pipeline automation, thereby reducing operational effort, delivery times, and costs. Attendees will gain a concrete understanding of what AgentOps is, how to start designing useful agent-based architectures, which patterns to apply, and how to turn this trend into a real advantage for technology, product, and business teams.

name: Marcos Martinez
title: The Model Was the Easy Part: Shipping LLM Order Processing at a CPG Company
abstract: A midsize US consumer packaged goods company (around 400 employees ) received about 100 purchase orders a day, all by email. Eight full-time employees did one thing: reading those orders, extracting fields, validating data, and typing it into downstream systems. With the business looking to scale its operations, we replaced that process with an LLM-powered pipeline, and learned that the model was the easy part. One early constraint shaped everything: email had to stay. With that many clients, each with their own habits and formats, you can't force a channel migration overnight , a customer portal is being built in parallel, but adoption takes time. So the pipeline had to meet the business where it was: unstructured PDFs and spreadsheets arriving in an inbox. This talk walks through what it took to ship: structured extraction with strict schemas where prompt and schema can't drift apart; per-field prompt rules ("verbatim or null", "never compute totals") where each clause exists because an eval caught the error class it kills; and confidence-scored human-in-the-loop review, because 90% field accuracy means designing for the other 10%. Not everything in an AI project is agents and models. A large part of the work is making the AI coexist with the systems and data a business already runs on: a legacy ERP accessible only through a remote-desktop VDI, undocumented APIs, unsynced environments, and an analytics database repurposed for things it was never designed to do. We'll also tour the engineering patterns that shape a pipeline like this in the real world: prompt caching for cost optimization, parallelization against real-world rate limits, batch processing when latency isn't actually a requirement, LLM-emitted confidence scores calibrated against ground truth, email classification to filter out false positives, and review-and-retry passes with a second model. And the one lesson that changed how we measure everything: evaluate per category, not just in aggregate, an 80% overall score can hide a client stuck at 33%, and the road to full automation runs through finding them. With versioned ground-truth evals, even swapping models becomes a measured decision instead of a leap of faith, because when the engineering around it is right, the specific model matters less than you'd think. Attendees will leave with a concrete blueprint for taking an LLM extraction system from promising demo to production system a business actually depends on.

name: Martin Brian
title: The Harness Auction: What Makes an AI Agent Actually Work?
abstract: What makes an AI agent effective: a better model, the right tools, specialized skills, more context, subagents, or a verification loop? In this interactive talk, every audience member receives a limited budget and bids in a live auction for the components needed to assemble an agent harness. Participants then lock in their chosen combination and watch it enter a controlled benchmark gauntlet measuring correctness, regressions, safe execution, speed, and cost until only the winning harness remains.Through the results, we will explore which components materially improve an agent, which merely add cost and complexity, and why the system surrounding an LLM can matter as much as the model itself.
bio: Martin Brian is a Senior AI Engineer specializing in the design, deployment, and operation of agentic systems in demanding production environments. At Marvik, he works as part of the AI team for a global payments platform, building agents that automate end-to-end software-development workflows across the organization.
